title: Mishpatim: the widow and the orphan (Exodus 22:21–23)
hook: God hears the cry of the widow and the fatherless
tomorrow: Mishpatim: we will do, and we will hear (Exodus 24:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Mishpatim, the law of your enemy's fallen donkey. Your line was help your enemy's donkey. Today, the people with nobody to help them.

In an office there can be someone no one stands up for: the temp, the new hire with no friends yet, the cleaner who comes in after everyone's gone. If someone takes advantage of them, who will complain? Who will even notice? In the ancient world, the people in that position had names. A widow, with no husband to speak for her in court. An orphan, with no father to protect his inheritance. Easy people to cheat. The Torah turns to them directly, and does something unusual: it names who is listening.
screen: `THE ONE NOBODY STANDS UP FOR.` → `THE WIDOW AND THE ORPHAN.` → `WHO IS LISTENING?`

segments.voice: Here's the law, in the old Jewish translation: "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." Then: if you afflict them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry. In Hebrew, three verbs in that line are doubled. Afflict, you afflict. Cry, they cry. Hear, I will hear. It's the Hebrew way of saying: really, surely, I mean it. The next verse is fierce. It warns that the one who harms them will meet the same fate, their own wives widowed, their own children fatherless. Measure for measure. The Torah doesn't soften it, and this lesson won't either. Rashi asks a fair question. Is it only widows and orphans you mustn't afflict? No, he says, following the Mekhilta: the same law covers every person. The Torah names these two because they're the weakest and the easiest to hurt. The law speaks where the danger is greatest. Who has no protection now? A tenant without a lease. An elderly person living alone. A child in foster care. A worker far from home. The categories change; the shape doesn't. And notice where the verse puts God: not on the side of the powerful, the judge or the landowner, but at the ear of the person crying. Isaiah picks this up, telling Israel to judge the fatherless and plead for the widow.
screen: `YE SHALL NOT AFFLICT ANY WIDOW.` · `DOUBLED VERBS: SURELY I WILL HEAR.` · `RASHI: EVERYONE, BUT THE WEAKEST FIRST.` · `WHO HAS NO PROTECTION NOW?` · then, large: `GOD HEARS THEM.`

segments.voice: Let one person around you who has nobody to speak for them come into focus: an older neighbor living alone, a new coworker, a kid at the edge of the playground. What do they need that they can't ask for? If you pray, you can hold them before God, who the verse says surely hears; if not, simply listen, the way you'd want someone to listen to you.
Mishpatim. The ordinances. Today, the law that protects the widow and the fatherless, and says God surely hears their cry.
Your line: God hears them. The quietest cry is the one the verse names. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish communities have kept funds and societies for widows, orphans and the poor, and Jewish law, following Rashi and the Mekhilta, applies the ban on afflicting the widow and orphan to every person, with special care for the vulnerable.
